earlier_scan.source_named: Kutsch Lojenga, Constance. 2003. Bila (D32). In Nurse & Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages. Routledge (phonology sketch; not freely online)

new_statements.quote: 2.3 Tone Bila being a Bantu language, one would expect to find a two-tone system with or without downstep. However, when making a first attempt at analysing nouns and verbs in isola-tion, it appears that […] My conclusion is therefore that Bila has three underlying tones synchronically, High, Mid, and Low, which I call High (H, acute accent), Low (L, zero marking), and extra-Low (xL, grave accent) respectively, for the sake of comparison with the neighboring languages Komo and Bhele. In addition to the three level tones, there […] In addition, Bila also has downstep of H tone, though not as a result of H-spreading and subsequent delinking of L tones, but in certain grammatical environments […]
new_statements.citation: Kutsch Lojenga, Constance. 2003. Bila (D32). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu languages, 450-474. London/New York: Routledge.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Tone (within §2 Phonology, pp. 450-474; exact page not recoverable from search snippets, probably c. pp. 453-455 since §1 Introduction runs pp. 450-452 per Glottolog and §3 Nominal morphology begins before p. 463 per Grambank)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bila is described as a three-tone language (H, L, extra-Low) with grammatical downstep; the sketch's phonology section (vowels/ATR harmony, consonants, tone) says nothing about word stress or accentual prominence. No fixed-position or weight-based stress rule is given because none is claimed.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement). Tonal note: downstep of H arises in certain grammatical environments, not from H-spreading; author suggests Bila once had a two-tone system with downstep like Komo and Bhele.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone analysis based on nouns and verbs in isolation (citation forms); no word- vs phrase-level stress discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Kutsch Lojenga 2003 describes Bila (Forest Bira, bila1255; Bombi and Nyaku as the main varieties, Kaiku a third), spoken around Mambasa and Lolwa; not to be confused with Bera/plains Bira (bera1259, Meinhof 1938/39) or Kango/Sua Pygmy varieties (kang1285). The quoted tone statement is about Bila proper.
